title: Bee treatment
subtitle: Based on Mitch's answers and the product labels, checked against NSW requirements. Updated 6 Nov 2026.
source: Mitch's answers 6 Nov 2026; jobbook-data/chemicals.json (Wasp/Bee Treatment products); jobbook-data/services.json (past wordings); LPC Tech Onboarding Pack (PPE, never list); sting first aid from ASCIA and Healthdirect guidance and bee versus wasp questions from Australian Museum and CSIRO guidance (not from Mitch)

sections.heading: When this job comes up
body: Customer has bees. Mitch's service is called Wasp/Bee Treatment (wasps and bees share one service). Past invoices read: "Treated active bee infestation".

The bees Mitch treats are honey bees, usually in wall cavities, eaves and similar spots. Mitch prefers the customer uses a beekeeper, but it is up to the owner. Leave other native bees alone and call Mitch.
Mortar bee (in brickwork) can be treated too. Mitch will show you how on the ride-along. Until then, follow the product label.

Bees also turn up as a finding on inspections, for example an active bee infestation in a gable, or mortar bee activity in brickwork. For an active bee infestation the report tells the customer to contact Mitch if they want it treated.
The job process, the never list, PPE and the free service period are in the Every job guide.

sections.heading: What the law and the label require

items.text: Follow the product label
items.detail: Using a pesticide against its label is an offence. If the job needs something the label does not allow, stop and call Mitch.

items.text: Make the record the same day
items.detail: Every pesticide job needs a record: full product name, date, target pest, rate and quantity, address and area treated, who applied it, equipment, and start and finish times. It must be made within 48 hours and kept at least 3 years. Give the customer a copy if they ask.

items.text: Only do work your licence covers
items.detail: If a treatment is outside your licence class, work under Mitch's direct supervision and do not do it alone.

items.text: Protect people, pets and the environment
items.detail: Wear the PPE the label and SDS call for. Keep spray and bait away from people, pets, food, drains and waterways. Harming people, wildlife or property with a pesticide is an offence.

items.text: Roof voids and subfloors: asbestos
items.detail: Houses built before 1990 can have asbestos (roof insulation, eaves, cladding). Do not disturb anything that might be asbestos. Stop and tell Mitch.

items.text: Roof voids: live wiring
items.detail: Look first. Do not touch cables. If you are not sure it is safe, do not go in and tell Mitch.

items.text: Tight or stuffy spaces
items.detail: If you cannot get out easily, or the air feels wrong, do not go in. Tell Mitch first.

items.text: Ladders and heights
items.detail: Work from the ground where you can. Never stand on the top two steps. Keep three points of contact. All four feet down. Tie extension ladders off top and bottom.

sections.heading: Ask about allergies first
sections.body: Ask BEFORE you start. Ask the customer, and anyone else at the property, if anyone is allergic to stings.
items: Most stings are not too bad. If someone is allergic, it means an epi-pen and hospital.
Ask about allergies before you start. If anyone at the property is allergic, call Mitch before you treat. Keep them away from the area and make sure their medication is on hand.

sections.heading: PPE
sections.title: PPE on before you go in
sections.note: Never apply chemicals without PPE. If the SDS requires it, you wear it. No exceptions.

items.text: Bee suit for all bee treatment
items.detail: Mitch's answer for bees.

items: Gloves and closed shoes at minimum
Gloves, mask and eye protection for any spray or dust, as per the product SDS

items.text: Roof void entry: dust mask, gloves, torch, appropriate footwear
Subfloor entry: coveralls, gloves, dust mask, torch

rows: Usually this. Blown into the cavity with the powder blower.
Mitch usually uses Coopex dust for bees.

sections.heading: Steps
sections.title: Steps
items: Ask if anyone at the property is allergic to stings, before you start
Ask the customer to point out where the bees are and where they are going in and out
Take BEFORE photos of the area
Suit up in the bee suit

items.text: Look for a way into the cavity
items.detail: Drill access holes only if it is needed and the owner allows it.

items.text: Treat the hive with Coopex, blown into the cavity with the powder blower
items.detail: Any time of day is fine. Stand wherever you need to work, in the bee suit.

items.text: Keep the customer and pets away from the area while you treat
items.detail: Keep the customer and pets inside, away from the nest area, while you treat.

items.text: Do not remove the comb or the hive
items.detail: We do not remove it. A beekeeper, a builder or a chippy opens up the wall for that.

items.text: Apply per the product label. Never exceed label rates
items.detail: Never mix chemicals without checking the label first. If in doubt, call Mitch.

items: Keep chemicals away from food, children and pets
Note anything you could not treat or reach, and why
Take AFTER photos

sections.heading: Bee or wasp? Questions for the phone

items.text: What does it look like?
items.detail: Honey bees are furry and brownish, with dull yellow and brown bands, about 1.3 to 1.6 cm long. Wasps have fewer hairs and a narrow waist.

items.text: Are they carrying yellow pollen on their back legs?
items.detail: Pollen bags on the back legs mean a bee.

items.text: Where are they going in and out, and what does the nest look like?
items.detail: A papery nest of open cells hanging from an eave or branch is a paper wasp nest.

items: Has anyone been stung, and is anyone allergic?

sections.heading: If someone is stung

items.text: Watch for a severe allergic reaction
items.detail: Difficult or noisy breathing, swelling of the tongue or throat, wheeze or a cough that will not stop, a hoarse voice, dizziness or collapse. After an insect sting, tummy pain or vomiting counts too.

items.text: If you see any of those: lay them flat, use an adrenaline device if there is one, and call 000
items.detail: Do not let them stand or walk. If breathing is hard they can sit with their legs out. If in doubt, give the adrenaline. Everyone who has a reaction like this needs to go to hospital.

items.text: Ordinary sting: scrape out the sting, wash with soap and water, then a cold pack wrapped in a cloth for 15 minutes
items.detail: A honey bee leaves its sting in the skin. Scrape it out with a fingernail edge or a card. Do not squeeze it.

items.text: Get medical help straight away for a sting in the mouth, or on the neck or face, or lots of stings
items.detail: Lots means 5 or more for a child, 10 or more for an adult.

items: Not sure? Poisons Information Centre on 13 11 26, from anywhere in Australia
Then call Mitch and write down what happened

sections.heading: Job complete when
items: BEFORE and AFTER photos taken
Bees treated
Anything you could not treat or reach is noted on the job report, with the reason
Product, rate, area and quantity recorded on the job report
Customer told what you did, and that we do not remove the comb or hive, and that the comb left behind can attract cockroaches and other pests. A beekeeper or builder can open the wall to remove it.
Customer knows whether a second visit is needed (it depends on the job and the access)
Customer given the re-entry time
Service report left, or customer told it is being emailed

items.q: Why does it need doing now?
items.a: It is best to get onto it early. If they are left, they will build a hive in the wall. That brings moisture and sugars, and it attracts cockroaches.

items.q: Can you take the hive or the honey out?
items.a: No, we do not remove the comb or the hive. A beekeeper, a builder or a chippy opens up the wall for that.

items.q: Should I get a beekeeper instead?
items.a: We prefer a beekeeper, but it is up to you.

items.q: Will you need to drill my wall?
items.a: Only if we need to, to get into the cavity, and only if you allow it.

items.q: Will you need to come back?
items.a: It depends on the job and the access. Sometimes yes, sometimes no.

sections.heading: Tell Mitch straight away if
sections.body: Call Mitch on 0432 181 689. After hours or urgent, call Mitch directly.

items.text: You apply the wrong chemical
items.detail: Stop immediately. Do not continue. Call Mitch.

items.text: There is a spill
items.detail: Follow the SDS procedure. Call Mitch immediately. Never leave a spill unattended.

items.text: Someone is hurt
items.detail: Treat the injury first (see If someone is stung above). Call Mitch. Write down what happened.

items.text: The customer complains or gets aggressive
items.detail: Stay calm and do not argue. For a complaint, tell them Mitch will call them today. If they are aggressive, remove yourself. Call Mitch either way.

items.text: The customer asks for a quote on anything complex, or you are not sure
items.detail: Say "I'll need to get Mitch to come and have a look and provide a quote for that."

items.text: You see signs of termites or other pests outside this job
items.detail: Photograph it and tell Mitch. Termite quotes always go to Mitch.
